chunks: Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from al-Fadl ibn Shazaan, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz, from the one who informed him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

When you are in the obligatory prayer and you see a slave of yours who has absconded, or a debtor of yours upon whom is wealth (due to you), or a snake you fear for yourself, then cut off the prayer and pursue the slave, or your debtor, and kill the snake.
ai.seo_question: What are the valid reasons for breaking the obligatory prayer according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In al-Kafi, Shaykh al-Kulayni records this narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) to clarify the fiqh of *qat’ al-salah* (breaking the prayer) for urgent worldly matters. Unlike minor distractions that require completion, these specific scenarios—pursuing an absconding slave, recovering debt, or killing a feared snake—are deemed significant enough to justify interrupting the prayer, reflecting the Shia principle of balancing spiritual devotion with practical necessity and protection.

en.hubeali:
Muhammad Bin Ismail, from Al Fazl Bin Shazaan, from Hammad Bin Isa, from Hareyz, from the one who informed him, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘Whenever you are in the Obligatory Salāt and you see a slave of yours to have absconded, or a debtor of yours upon whom is wealth (due to you), or a snake you fear upon yourself, so cut off your Salāt and pursue the slave, or a debtor of yours, and kill the snake’.
en.sarwar: 5. Muhammad ibn ’Isma‘il has narrated from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan from Hammad ibn ‘Isa from Hariz from those who narrated to him who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘

When you are in obligatory Salah (prayer) and see your slave escaping or your debtor who owes you a certain amount of property, or a snake because of which you are afraid for your life, you can discontinue your Salah (prayer) follow the slave or debtor or kill the snake.’”
